children.text: A System That Forgets: The Reality of Healthcare Data Silos

Imagine that every time you moved to a new city, your entire life history — your relationships, your job experience, your education — was wiped from memory, and you had to start over as a stranger. In American healthcare, this happens to patients every single day. When a patient walks into an emergency department after a car accident, the physicians treating them often have no idea what medications they take, what allergies they have, or what chronic conditions they manage. When a specialist receives a referral, they may have no access to the primary care notes that explain why the patient was referred. When a patient is discharged from a hospital and transferred to a skilled nursing facility, the complete discharge summary may arrive days later — by fax.

This is the problem of healthcare interoperability, or more precisely, the lack of it. Healthcare interoperability is the ability of different health information systems, devices, and applications to access, exchange, integrate, and cooperatively use data in a coordinated way across organizational, regional, and national boundaries. The word is awkward and technical, but the stakes could not be more human. When health data cannot follow the patient, the patient becomes the most error-prone link in their own care chain — forced to recall complex medication regimens from memory, repeat procedures they have already undergone, and navigate a system that treats every encounter as if it were the first.

The U.S. healthcare system has spent decades and hundreds of billions of dollars building electronic health records, imaging archives, laboratory systems, pharmacy networks, and insurance platforms — yet these systems are largely isolated from one another, unable to communicate seamlessly. Each island of data is technically sophisticated in isolation; together, they form a fragmented archipelago that fails patients at precisely the moments when continuity of information matters most: during emergencies, care transitions, and the management of complex chronic conditions.

body.analogy: Think of the U.S. healthcare data landscape as a country where every city speaks a different language and uses a different currency. Within each city, commerce works fine. But the moment you try to travel from one city to another, the system breaks down. A prescription written in Boston is illegible in Phoenix. A lab result from a community clinic is unreadable by the hospital two miles away. No single traveler — or patient — can be fully served.

children.text: The Financial Toll: Billions Lost to Administrative Friction and Duplication

The financial cost of poor interoperability is staggering, even by the standards of a system that routinely deals in trillions of dollars. CAQH, which tracks administrative efficiency across the healthcare industry, reported in its 2025 Index that the U.S. healthcare system still has a remaining $21 billion annual savings opportunity from fully automating manual and partially manual administrative transactions — tasks like eligibility verification, prior authorization, claims, and referrals — that are currently slowed or blocked by data systems that cannot talk to each other. Notably, the same research showed that over the past decade, the industry has avoided an estimated $258 billion in administrative costs through increased electronic automation — a remarkable achievement that also illustrates how much had been wasted before.

Prior authorization alone consumes an extraordinary share of clinical and administrative resources. Because payers and providers use different data systems that do not share information automatically, staff at physician offices must manually retrieve patient history, compile supporting clinical documentation, and submit requests through proprietary payer portals — often by phone or fax. The CAQH research found that the average time saved per patient visit when providers use fully automated administrative workflows is 70 minutes. Multiply that by hundreds of millions of patient visits annually, and the scale of reclaimed clinical capacity becomes vivid. That is time physicians and nurses could spend with patients rather than navigating bureaucratic systems designed for a pre-digital era.

Duplicate testing is another enormous and well-documented cost driver directly tied to interoperability failure. When a patient's prior laboratory results are inaccessible to a new treating physician, the physician has no choice but to reorder tests already performed. A landmark study published in BMC Medical Informatics found that duplication of testing — defined as a repeat within 12 hours — occurred in 32% of cases examined, with 20% of cases having at least one test that was clinically unindicated. Across the system, redundant testing alone is estimated to waste up to $5 billion annually in the United States. These are not abstractions. They are real resources — physician time, technician effort, reagents, imaging machine capacity, and patient inconvenience — consumed repeatedly by the same system failure.

Duplicate and redundant medical testing — driven largely by inaccessible prior records — wastes an estimated $5 billion per year in the United States, according to research published in BMC Medical Informatics and affiliated studies.

children.text: The Human Cost: Patient Safety Failures When Data Cannot Follow the Patient

The financial costs of poor interoperability, as significant as they are, pale in comparison to the human costs. The most consequential failures happen not to spreadsheets, but to people. When health data does not flow with the patient, clinicians are forced to make decisions under conditions of preventable ignorance — and preventable ignorance causes preventable harm.

Medication safety is one of the clearest casualties. The World Health Organization estimates that medication errors cost approximately $42 billion annually worldwide and account for 1% of total global health expenditure. In the United States, approximately six percent of hospitalizations are attributable to medication allergies known to cause adverse drug reactions. Many of these are not mysterious or unforeseeable events; they are cases where the allergy was documented somewhere in the healthcare system, but the system treating the patient at that moment had no access to that documentation. AHRQ's PSNet has published case studies of medication-induced hemolytic reactions in patients with clearly documented allergies that were simply invisible to the treating facility because the information lived in a different, non-interoperable EHR.

Incomplete records create a broader pattern of harm that researchers have documented across care settings. Studies of primary care incident reports find that nearly half of all patient safety incidents related to information flow involved inadequate, missing, or incorrect information. One analysis found 18 documented cases of serious patient harm directly attributable to patient data management and documentation failures in a single study period. Nearly all adverse events in one major study were classified as preventable — meaning the harm would not have occurred if the right information had been available to the right clinician at the right time.

body.content: A patient is stabilized at a rural emergency department after a cardiac event and transferred to a regional hospital for catheterization. The transfer arrives with a paper summary; the detailed EHR record, including a recent echocardiogram and a complex medication reconciliation from an outpatient cardiologist, is unavailable because the originating and receiving hospitals use different EHR systems with no active health information exchange. The receiving team must repeat several diagnostic steps, delay the procedure, and administer a medication that interacts with the patient's existing regimen — all because the data did not travel with the patient. This is not a hypothetical; it is the daily operational reality for a majority of U.S. hospitals.
body.title: A Real Pattern: The Transferred Patient

body.message: As of 2023, ONC data showed that only 70% of U.S. hospitals performed all four core interoperability functions: electronically sending, receiving, finding, and integrating health information. That means roughly 30% of American hospitals still cannot reliably perform one or more of these basic data exchange functions — leaving millions of patients at risk when they move across care settings.

children.text: The Revolving Door: How Data Gaps Drive Preventable Hospital Readmissions

Care transitions — the handoffs between care settings when patients move from hospital to home, from primary care to specialist, from emergency department to observation unit — are the most dangerous moments in a patient's healthcare journey. They are dangerous precisely because they require seamless data flow, and that seamless data flow frequently does not exist.

Hospital readmissions are the most measurable symptom of care transition failure. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) operates the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP), which penalizes hospitals financially for excess readmissions within 30 days of discharge for conditions including heart failure, pneumonia, and hip/knee replacement. In 2024, 70% of U.S. hospitals faced financial penalties under this program — a figure that underscores how pervasive care transition failures remain. These are not isolated failures at poorly managed institutions; they are system-wide indicators of what happens when discharge information, medication reconciliation, and follow-up care instructions do not reliably reach the next provider in the chain.

Research has directly linked health information exchange participation to reduced readmission rates. A study published in Health Affairs found that HIE participation was associated with a 1.3 percentage point greater reduction in the probability of unplanned 30-day readmissions for acute myocardial infarction compared to non-participating hospitals. Systematic reviews of HIE outcomes have consistently found that when clinical data can travel across organizational boundaries, hospitals admit fewer patients unnecessarily, emergency departments are used more appropriately, and the overall cost of care declines.

The mechanism is straightforward: when a discharging hospital can electronically notify a primary care physician of a patient's discharge, share the complete medication list, flag pending follow-up tests, and transmit the discharge summary in a structured format the receiving system can read — the likelihood of a patient falling through the cracks drops substantially. When that information arrives by fax three days later, or not at all, the patient is left to navigate the transition alone, often with incomplete understanding of their own treatment plan.

children.text: COVID-19: When Interoperability Failures Become a National Emergency

The COVID-19 pandemic of 2020-2021 provided an unprecedented stress test of the U.S. healthcare data infrastructure — and the results were sobering. The pandemic revealed with stark clarity what public health officials and health informaticists had been warning about for years: that fragmented, non-interoperable health data systems were not merely inefficient but genuinely dangerous at the population scale.

Case reporting — the foundational public health function of knowing where a disease is spreading and how fast — was crippled by data fragmentation. Across federal, state, and local jurisdictions, data platforms used different definitions, different formats, and different transmission mechanisms. A case reported to a state health department in one format could not automatically flow to a CDC system expecting a different format. The result was that public health officials were making containment and resource allocation decisions based on data that was days or weeks out of date, incomplete in geographic coverage, and systematically missing demographic information on race and ethnicity that was critical for identifying and addressing disparate community impacts.

Vaccination record management proved equally problematic. Many primary care practices were unable to reliably capture vaccination status or receive vaccination data from the immunization information systems operated by states — systems that were themselves fragmented and often unable to exchange data across state lines. Patients who received their first vaccine dose in one state and their second dose in another created records that often could not be reconciled. Healthcare workers administering vaccines frequently had no electronic visibility into a patient's prior vaccination history.

A subsequent analysis published in Health Affairs Scholar documented that hospitals faced significant challenges in COVID-19 public health reporting due to interoperability gaps in their data exchange infrastructure. Research published in PMC identified that the fundamental problem was not a lack of data, but a lack of data infrastructure capable of aggregating, standardizing, and sharing that data in real time. The pandemic did not create these fragmentation problems; it revealed them — at a cost measured not in dollars, but in lives.

The COVID-19 pandemic exposed a hard truth: a healthcare system that cannot share data seamlessly in routine times will fail catastrophically under stress. Interoperability is not a technical nicety — it is a foundational requirement of public health resilience.
The Policy Response: How ONC and CMS Are Mandating a Better Future

Recognizing the scale of the problem, the federal government has made healthcare interoperability a central policy priority over the past decade. The legislative foundation is the 21st Century Cures Act of 2016, which directed both the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC) and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) to take concrete regulatory action to advance interoperability and prohibit practices that block the flow of health information.

ONC's Cures Act Final Rule, finalized in 2020, established several landmark requirements. It mandated that EHR vendors adopt standardized application programming interfaces (APIs) based on the HL7 FHIR standard, enabling patients and authorized third-party applications to access structured electronic health information at no cost. It prohibited "information blocking" — practices by health IT developers, health networks, or providers that unreasonably prevent or interfere with the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information. Penalties for information blocking can reach up to $1 million per violation for certified health IT developers, with provider-facing disincentives tied to federal payment programs.

CMS reinforced these requirements through its Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule, which required Medicare and Medicaid payers to implement FHIR-based APIs giving patients electronic access to their claims and clinical data. The Payer-to-Payer Data Exchange rule extended this further, requiring health plans to share patient clinical information with new plans when patients change coverage — addressing a long-standing gap where years of clinical history would simply disappear when a patient switched insurers.

These policy mandates reflect a recognition that market forces alone have proven insufficient to drive interoperability. Individual health systems and EHR vendors have historically had financial incentives to retain patient data within their networks rather than share it with competitors. Regulation has been necessary to override those incentives and establish a floor of data-sharing behavior that the entire system must meet. ONC's stated goal is a future in which any patient can securely access, share, and use all of their electronic health information, regardless of where that information was created or by whom.

children.text: What the Evidence Shows: The Proven Benefits of Interoperability

Beyond documenting the costs of fragmentation, a growing body of research demonstrates the concrete benefits that emerge when health information can actually flow across organizational boundaries. These studies provide the evidence base for the policy investments and regulatory mandates that have defined the past decade of health IT policy.

The Health Affairs study on HIE and acute myocardial infarction readmissions is representative of a consistent research finding: when clinical information travels with the patient, outcomes improve and costs fall. Systematic reviews of HIE outcomes published in JMIR Medical Informatics and the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association have found that HIE participation is associated with fewer duplicate procedures, reduced imaging orders, lower emergency department costs, and improved ambulatory quality of care. Studies with more rigorous research designs consistently report benefits across these domains.

The 2025 CAQH Index provides perhaps the most comprehensive quantitative picture of what improved data exchange has already achieved administratively: an estimated $258 billion in administrative costs avoided through electronic transactions over the measurement period, with a documented 70-minute time savings per patient visit when fully automated administrative workflows are in place. This is time returned to clinical care — to the patient-physician relationship — rather than to administrative overhead.

Population health management is another domain where interoperability pays measurable dividends. When a health system can aggregate clinical data across all of its patients — including data from outside its own walls — it can identify high-risk patients before they deteriorate, coordinate proactive outreach, and target care management resources where they will have the greatest impact. These capabilities depend entirely on the ability to access and integrate data from multiple sources: EHRs, labs, pharmacies, social determinants screening tools, and payer claims feeds. Interoperability is the infrastructure on which population health rests.

When clinical information travels with the patient, outcomes improve, costs fall, and clinicians can focus on care rather than the search for missing data. Interoperability is not a technology project — it is the prerequisite for a functioning healthcare system.
Key Takeaways

points: Poor healthcare interoperability imposes an estimated $21 billion in remaining annual administrative waste, with redundant testing alone costing up to $5 billion per year in the United States.
Nearly half of all patient safety incidents related to information flow involve missing, inadequate, or incorrect information — and the vast majority of adverse events are considered preventable.
Medication errors tied to missing allergy and medication history cost an estimated $42 billion annually worldwide and drive approximately 6% of U.S. hospitalizations.

In 2024, 70% of U.S. hospitals faced financial penalties under CMS's readmissions reduction program — a direct measure of how frequently care transitions fail when data does not travel with the patient.

Research in Health Affairs found that HIE participation reduces 30-day readmission rates for heart attack patients by 1.3 percentage points — demonstrating that better data exchange produces measurable clinical improvements.

The COVID-19 pandemic exposed systemic interoperability failures in case reporting, vaccination records, and demographic data collection, revealing that fragmented data infrastructure is a public health risk, not merely an administrative inconvenience.

The 21st Century Cures Act, ONC's Cures Act Final Rule, and CMS's Interoperability and Patient Access Rule represent the largest federal regulatory push in history to mandate FHIR-based data sharing and prohibit information blocking.

Interoperability is not a technical end goal in itself — it is the infrastructure prerequisite for safe care transitions, effective population health management, clinical decision support, and a patient experience that respects continuity across a lifetime of care.

The $258 billion figure refers to costs already avoided through electronic automation over the prior measurement period, while $5 billion estimates annual duplicate testing waste and $42 billion is the WHO's estimate of global annual medication error costs.
